### 1) Is Multi-Valued Attributes Synching from On-Premises AD to Azure AD Supported?

The short answer is that the default behavior of Azure AD Connect doesn't support multi-valued attributes from on-premises AD to Azure AD by default. Azure AD Connect is primarily designed for syncing single-valued attributes, such as user and group memberships, email addresses, phone numbers, and more. Multi-valued attributes, which can be things like department, preferred language, or custom fields, are not typically supported out-of-the-box.

### 2) How to Know if an Attribute is Single or Multi-Valued in Azure AD Connect

In Azure AD Connect, you can check the attributes to see if they are single-valued or multi-valued. Here’s how you can do it:

- **Open Azure AD Connect:** Log in to the Azure AD Connect service and open the Azure AD Connect module.
  
- **Navigate to the Directory Extensions Page:**
  - Go to the "Directory Extensions" section.
  - Here, you can see a list of the attributes that are being synchronized.

- **Check the Attribute Type:**
  - Look for the attribute in the list of syncable attributes.
  - On the right side of the attribute, it should show the type of synchronization it is being configured for. If it says "Single Value" or "Single", it means the attribute is being synced as a single value.
  - If it says "Multi Value" or "Multi", it means the attribute is being synced as a multi-value attribute.

### Additional Considerations

If you need to sync multi-valued attributes, you will need to manually configure it using Azure AD Connect’s PowerShell cmdlets or the Azure AD Connect PowerShell module. Here’s a brief overview of how to do this:

- **PowerShell:**
  ```powershell
  Connect-AzureAD -Environment "AzureChinaCloud"
  Get-AzureADMSSyncedObjectExtensionAttribute -ObjectId "userObjectId" -ObjectType "User"
  ```

- **Azure AD Connect PowerShell Module:**
  ```powershell
  Import-Module AzureADConnect

  Get-AzureADDirectorySyncEnabledAttribute | Where-Object { $_.Name -like "*YourAttribute*" }
  ```

### Conclusion

To summarize, while Azure AD Connect syncs single-valued attributes by default, multi-valued attributes are not supported natively. You will need to manually configure the synchronization of multi-valued attributes using PowerShell or Azure AD Connect’s built-in features. This manual configuration will allow you to sync multi-valued attributes from on-premises Active Directory to Azure AD.

title: Flow control on a FT232RL
ground_truth_answer:
TL;DR

According to the FTDI documentation the default configuration of pin CBUS2 is TXDEN, which is expressly designed for this feature, so just use pin CBUS2 for your transceiver enable.

Background

The FTDI chip is certainly capable of DTR/DSR flow control.

But that is for when the hardware handles the flow control by itself (communicating with the far end, which can provide back pressure). No software involvement is required.

With a multidrop bus like RS485, the actual flow control is handled in software, and hardware just sends data when directed by the software.

As one of your commenters suggests, you could write additional software to turn DTR on, send data, and turn DTR back off. But that is problematic for meeting tight timing, and there is no actual need for that, because the FTDI chip has support for turning the transmitter on for you, based on when you are sending data. This support may or may not be available on the DTR signal you are using, though.

FTDI's name of the signal which can control a transceiver is TXDEN. Depending on which FTDI chip you are using, this could be routed to one of a few different pins.

To set that routing up, you simply run FTDI's FT_Prog. You can scan and parse the current devices, and then make changes using a GUI. You can save and restore configurations from XML files as well. The program will show you the routing options for TXDEN.

EDIT by ASKER:- This answer is complete with the following points:-

1) Download MPROG 3.5 as the programmer for the FTDI.

2) Select any one of programmable pins from any of the CBUS0 - CBUS4

3) Then after read and parse, change the selected pin to TXDEN and hit program

4) Do the necessary hardware connections for TXDEN

TXDEN is high till the FTDI is sending data and becomes low immediately and hence serves my purpose

title: How to do Basic Authentication using FireWatir on Ubuntu Linux?
ground_truth_answer:
With help from Aedorn Varanis I've got things working on Firefox in Linux.

Aedorn sent me a "logon" method which issues a jssh command that checks for an "Authentication Required" dialog and if it exists, fills in the username/password and submits the dialog.

I've copied and pasted what he sent me below:

You use a method that looks like this:

def logon(username, password, wait=3)
        jssh_command = "var length = getWindows().length; var win;var found=false; for(var i = 0; i < length; i++) { win = getWindows()[i]; if(win.document.title == \"Authentication Required\") { found = true; break; }} if(found) { var jsdocument = win.document; var dialog = jsdocument.getElementsByTagName(\"dialog\")[0];"
        jssh_command << " jsdocument.getElementsByTagName(\"textbox\")[0].value = \"#{username}\";"
        jssh_command << " jsdocument.getElementsByTagName(\"textbox\")[1].value = \"#{password}\";"
        jssh_command << " dialog.getButton(\"accept\").click(); }\n"
        sleep(wait)
        $jssh_socket.send(jssh_command,0)
        read_socket()
        wait()
end

Then you can call it within its own thread just before going to the site with the login requirement:

Thread.new { logon(user, pass) }
@ff.goto("http://some_url.com")
sleep 3

Increase the wait and sleep time if the page takes awhile to load. If your main process tries to run while the command is being sent through the JSSH socket, it will stall and sit there forever until killed. Also, there's no real way to detect if the authentication window comes up. That means you need to make sure it always works the same way every time, or it, too, causes problems. Finally, the method will always have to be in another thread, because once the authentication window comes up, it stops all other processing until it goes away. Other than that, it works.

From this, I was able to subclass the FireWatir::Firefox class with a new Browser class which supports a "credentials=" method just like the Celerity::Browser does. So, just like using celerity, you can do:

require 'browser'
browser = Browser.new
browser.credentials = 'user:pass'
browser.goto('http://some.basic.auth.url')

This will automatically fill in the Basic Auth dialog and log you into the site.

I've posted the contents of my browser.rb file below (notice this works in ruby+firewatir and jruby+celerity in linux): 

ENGINE = defined?(RUBY_ENGINE) ? RUBY_ENGINE : 'ruby'
if ENGINE == 'ruby'
  require 'firewatir'

  class Browser < FireWatir::Firefox

    def initialize(options={})
      super(options)
      @username = nil
      @password = nil
    end

    def credentials=(string)
      username, password = string.split(":")
      if username.nil? or password.nil?
        raise "Invalid credentials: #{string})"
      else
        @username = username
        @password = password
      end
    end

    def goto(url, wait=3)
      if @username.nil? and @password.nil?
        return super(url)
      else
        t = Thread.new { logon(@username, @password, wait) }
        result = super(url)
        t.join
        return result
      end
    end

    private

    def logon(username, password, wait)
      jssh_command = "
        var length = getWindows().length;
        var win;
        var found = false;
        for (var i = 0; i < length; i++) {
          win = getWindows()[i];
          if(win.document.title == \"Authentication Required\") {
            found = true;
            break;
          }
        }
        if (found) {
          var jsdocument = win.document;
          var dialog = jsdocument.getElementsByTagName(\"dialog\")[0];
          jsdocument.getElementsByTagName(\"textbox\")[0].value = \"#{username}\";
          jsdocument.getElementsByTagName(\"textbox\")[1].value = \"#{password}\";
          dialog.getButton(\"accept\").click();
        }
      \n"
      sleep(wait)
      $jssh_socket.send(jssh_command,0)
      read_socket()
    end
  end
elsif ENGINE == 'jruby'
  require 'celerity'
  class Browser < Celerity::Browser; end
else
  raise "Ruby ENGINE '#{ENGINE}' not supported."
end

title: Image resizing program outputs a distorted image
ground_truth_answer:
You are reading input for each repeated horizontal line, which is why the square moved up.

It should be moved out of the vertical scale loop. I suggest you allocate memory for one scan line, read the whole line into a buffer, and then write it from the buffer.

// iterate over infile's scanlines

// TEMPORARY STORAGE
RGBTRIPLE *buff = malloc (bi.biWidth * sizeof(RGBTRIPLE));

for (int i = 0, biHeight = abs(bi.biHeight); i < biHeight; i++)
{
    // THIS MOVED UP OUT OF THE LOOP
    // read RGB triple from infile
    fread(buff, sizeof(RGBTRIPLE), bi.biWidth, inptr);

    for (int h = 0; h < scale; h++)
    {
        // iterate over pixels in scanline
        for (int j = 0; j < bi.biWidth; j++)
        {
            // write pixel per scale
            for (int w = 0; w < scale; w++)
            {
                // write RGB triple to outfile - FROM BUFFER
                fwrite(&buff[j], sizeof(RGBTRIPLE), 1, outptr);
            }
        }

        // then add it back (to demonstrate how)
        for (int k = 0; k < outpadding; k++)
        {
            fputc(0x00, outptr);
        }
    }
    // MOVED DOWN OUT OF LOOP
    // skip over padding, if any
    fseek(inptr, padding, SEEK_CUR);
}
free(buff);

The code should be checking the return value from fread, the number of items read. Because it does not, you failed to notice that no more data was being read, and your RGBTRIPLE triple continued to hold its previously read values.

    <xsl:copy>
        <xsl:apply-templates select="@*|*"/>
        <chapters>
            <chapter>
                <ch-name>default</ch-name>

            </chapter>

Certainly! The issue lies in your XSLT template. You're attempting to use `not(exists(chapters))` to determine whether a `chapters` element exists, but this is not directly supported in the XSLT syntax. 

Instead, you can use a template that matches the `book` elements that do not have a `chapters` element. Then, in the `xsl:apply-templates` statement, you can copy the book elements and then add a `chapters` element with the `default` child elements inside.

Here's the corrected XSLT:

```xml
<xsl:stylesheet version="1.0" xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
    <xsl:template match="book[not(chapters)]">
        <xsl:copy>
            <xsl:apply-templates select="@* | *"/>
            <chapters>
                <chapter>
                    <ch-name>default</ch-name>
                    <ch-number>default</ch-number>
                </chapter>
            </chapters>
        </xsl:copy>
    </xsl:template>

    <xsl:template match="@* | *">
        <xsl:copy>
            <xsl:apply-templates select="@* | * | text()"/>
        </xsl:copy>
    </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>
```

This XSLT will correctly add the `chapters` element with `default` child elements to the `book` elements that do not have a `chapters` element.

title: Build Mach-o file as encrypted
ground_truth_answer:
No, you cannot do this.

The only "supported" way of getting LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO added to your binary is by distributing through the iOS App Store. It is Apple who checks your binary for compliance with their rules, then encrypts the binary and re-signs it.

This is all backed by "FairPlay", Apple's proprietary DRM stack. Not much is known about it since the code is heavily obfuscated, but it is widely believed that it's built on features of Apple's custom hardware AES engine. Given this, it may or may not be possible to create an encryptor yourself, but it would require immense reverse engineering efforts to even find out.

Further, the entire FairPlay stack is only present on Apple's own chips. It is indeed available on M1 Macs, as you can install iOS apps off the shelf (so long as you leave SIP enabled), but it is not available at all on Intel Macs (the relevant kexts are IOTextEncryptionFamily.kext and FairPlayIOKit.kext, the latter of which is obfuscated).

The Mach-O file encryption you are referring to is a feature implemented by the macOS environment, but it is not something that can be achieved simply by modifying or re-signing an existing Mach-O file. Here's a brief explanation of how it works and why you might want to understand it:

### How Mach-O File Encryption Works

1. **Encryption Keys**: macOS uses a cryptographic algorithm to encrypt the code sections of an application. The keys for this encryption are stored in a special section of the Mach-O file, known as the `Section Load Address (SLA)` and `Section Segment (SS)` sections.

2. **Encryption Algorithm**: The encryption algorithm is part of the Mach-O file header, which is why it is referred to as "cryptographic" rather than just "encryption." The algorithm used is a specific implementation of the AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) algorithm.

3. **Key Storage**: The keys (master encryption key, user encryption key, and key storage key) are stored in the Mach-O file header. These keys are used to decrypt the encrypted code sections when the application runs.

4. **Code Sections**: The code sections of the Mach-O file (which are typically the `.text`, `.data`, and `.rdata` sections) are encrypted using these keys.

### Why You Can't Just Encrypt a Mach-O File

1. **Code Sections vs. Data Sections**: When you encrypt a Mach-O file, you are encrypting the code sections. However, macOS also encrypts the data sections (`.data`, `.rdata`, etc.) for security reasons. If you just encrypt the code sections, it could lead to the decryption of the data sections, which might not be secure.

2. **Header and Footer**: The encryption keys are stored at specific positions in the Mach-O file header and footer. Replacing one section without modifying the entire header and footer would result in the loss of the encryption keys, making the file invalid.

3. **Re-Signing**: Re-signing an application involves more than just encrypting. The app store signs the application for authenticity and updates. If you re-sign an application without changing the encryption keys, the signature might not be recognized by the app store.

### What You Can Do

1. **Use an App Store Bundle**: If you want to use encryption and re-sign your application, you should use an App Store Bundle. This allows you to use the `@rpath` mechanism to avoid changing the header and footer of the Mach-O file.

2. **Encrypt Code Sections**: You can encrypt the code sections (`.text`, `.data`, `.rdata`, etc.) by modifying the Mach-O file header and footer. However, you need to remember to update the keys stored at specific positions in the header and footer to maintain the integrity of the encryption.

3. **App Store Control**: The encryption keys are part of the app store signing process. If you re-sign an app without changing the encryption keys, the signature might not be recognized by the app store.

### Conclusion

While it is technically possible to encrypt a Mach-O file, it requires careful handling and adherence to the Apple's signing and encryption standards. Using an App Store Bundle is the best approach for achieving both encryption and re-signing in a secure manner.

title: Idiomatic Kotlin way to sum numbers from stdin until a condition is met
ground_truth_answer:
Your first function is fine, but it's written in an imperative style.  This is one of those cases where a functional style can be much more concise:

fun sumOfBigDecimals()
    = generateSequence(::readBigDecimal).reduce{ a, b -> a + b }

Hopefully this is fairly self-explanatory, but just in case:

The library function generateSequence builds a sequence (a lazy list), calling the given function for each new element, stopping when it returns null.

There's no general sum method we can use.  (sumBy() assumes that each value fits within an Int, so it doesn't support the arbitrary precision of BigDecimal.)  But we can easily build it using the reduce() function to add up consecutive values until there's only one left.

A slight variation on that is:

    = generateSequence(::readBigDecimal).reduce(BigDecimal::plus)

This uses a reference to the existing BigDecimal.plus() method to do the addition, instead of a lambda.  It takes a couple more characters, but may be marginally more efficient, and you may (or may not!) think it conceptually simpler.

(Your readBigDecimal() function is certainly using Kotlin idioms; it's a bit complex, but I can't immediately see any improvements.)
llm_answer:
Certainly! Let's approach this problem by optimizing the logic to avoid mutable state and using idiomatic Kotlin practices. Here are a few suggestions:

### 1. **Avoiding Mutable State:**
   - Instead of using a mutable variable `sum`, you can accumulate the sum directly using a `BigDecimal` instance.
   - The `while` loop can be simplified by directly processing the input without an intermediary variable.

### 2. **Simplifying the Read Function:**
   - Instead of `readLine()` and `let`, you can directly process `readLine()` without the extra null check.
   - Simplify the condition for `readLine()` and `readBigDecimal()`.

### 3. **Simplifying the Main Logic:**
   - Combine the logic to read and calculate the sum into a single function.

### Revised Code

Here's a cleaner version of the code:

```kotlin
fun sumOfBigDecimals() : BigDecimal {
    var sum = BigDecimal.ZERO
    while (true) {
        sum += readBigDecimal()
        if (sum <= BigDecimal.ZERO) break
    }
    return sum
}

fun readBigDecimal() = BigDecimal(readLine() ?: "0.0")

fun main() {
    val sum = sumOfBigDecimals()
    println(sum)
}
```

### Explanation:

1. **Simplified `readBigDecimal` Function:**
   - The `readBigDecimal` function now directly returns `BigDecimal` without a null check.
   - This is more readable and eliminates the need for `let`.

2. **Combined Logic in `sumOfBigDecimals`:**
   - The logic for reading and calculating the sum is combined into a single function.
   - The `while` loop now directly processes the `BigDecimal` returned by `readBigDecimal()`, eliminating the need for an intermediary variable.

3. **Breaking the Loop:**
   - The loop breaks when the sum is less than or equal to zero, which is a safer and more idiomatic way to stop the loop.

4. **Main Function:**
   - The `main` function simply calls `sumOfBigDecimals` and prints the result.

This approach makes the code more concise, readable, and idiomatically Kotlin.

title: Neo4j bulk import and indexing
ground_truth_answer:
Indexes are on Labels + Properties. You need indexes right after your import and before you start trying to optimize queries. Anything your query will use to find a starting point should be indexed (user_id, object_id, etc) and probably any dates or properties used for range queries (modified_on, weight, etc).

CREATE INDEX ON :Label(property)

Cypher queries are single threaded so I have no idea what you mean by multi-core support. What did you read about that, got a link? You can multi-thread Neo4j, but at this point you have to do it manually. See https://maxdemarzi.com/2017/01/06/multi-threading-a-traversal/

Most of the time, the queries can be greatly optimized with an index or expressing it differently. But sometimes you need to redo your model to fit the query. Take a look at https://maxdemarzi.com/2015/08/26/modeling-airline-flights-in-neo4j/ for some hints.
llm_answer:
Certainly! The neo4j bulk import tool allows you to import large amounts of data into your Neo4j instance without having to first create your indexes. However, creating indexes can be beneficial for performance, and there are methods you can use during the import process to ensure optimal performance.

### Creating Indexes During Bulk Import

When you use the `neo4j-import` tool, it is designed to import data quickly and efficiently, but it does not automatically create indexes. However, you can create indexes after the import is complete. Here’s how you can do it:

1. **After Import:**
   After you have finished importing your data and have optimized your queries, you can create indexes. This is generally the recommended approach because indexes are created during the import process, but they are not automatically available until after the import is complete.

   ```bash
   neo4j-import --import-tool neo4j-import --index CREATE INDEX ON :type;
   ```

   Replace `:type` with the actual label of your nodes.

2. **Creating Indexes During Import:**
   If you want to create indexes during the import process, you can use a separate script or the `neo4j-admin` tool. The `neo4j-admin` tool allows you to perform administrative tasks such as creating indexes during the import process.

   ```bash
   # Run the import script with administrative privileges
   ./neo4j-import --import-tool neo4j-import --allow-write --index CREATE INDEX ON :type;
   ```

   Again, replace `:type` with the actual label of your nodes.

### Creating a Statement for Every Node

If you want to create indexes for all nodes on a specific attribute (e.g., `type`), you can use the `CREATE INDEX` statement during the import process. However, you can do this in a more efficient manner by using the `neo4j-admin` tool, which can be used to create indexes in bulk.

```bash
# Create an index on all nodes of a specific type
neo4j-admin --allow-write index CREATE INDEX ON :type;
```

### Summary

- **Import with Indexes:**
  - After the import is complete, use `neo4j-import --index` to create indexes.
  
- **During Import with Indexes:**
  - Use the `neo4j-admin` tool to create indexes during the import process.

- **Optimizing Queries:**
  - After creating indexes, optimize your queries to ensure they are efficient. This includes profiling, multicore support, and splitting queries for better performance.

By following these steps, you can ensure that your indexes are created during the import process, which can significantly improve query performance.

  • Rhodes is the only framework with an app generator
  • Rhodes has broader OS support (including the only one with support for Windows Mobile)

  • Rhodes has true full IDE with an integrated debugger and a device independent simulator (something PhoneGap does not)

If you judge the framework by the ability to create a native app with HTML and make some device calls, PhoneGap and Rhodes are both pretty much the same. And both have few issues with bugs, as this low bar is fairly simple.

The differentiators listed above (which I summary as "modern development techniques for information intensive apps") have an inherent complexity to them. With the help of the community and a large dedicated QA staff from our new owner Motorola, these differentiator features are all now quite mature, and do not exist in other products.

Start by defining a couple subclasses:

public class StringPropertyValue : PropertyValue { }
public class BoolPropertyValue : PropertyValue { }
public class IntPropertyValue : PropertyValue { }
public class GuidsPropertyValue : PropertyValue { }

The names does not really matter because no special constraints are put on those classes, the only important thing is they to be different. We'll use those classes for projection instead of PropertyValue.

Then we'll need another simple class like this:

public class Property
{
    public PropertyValue Value { get; set; }
}

It's needed to workaround another EF limitation - unsupported casts. In order to project a PropertyValue, instead of unsupported

(PropertyValue)new StringPropertyValue { StringValue = .. }

we will perform the cast by using the ugly but supported

new Property { Value = new StringPropertyValue { StringValue = ... } }.Value

And that's it.

usersQuery
    .Where(u => new Property { Value = new StringPropertyValue {

    .Where(u => new Property { Value = new BoolPropertyValue {

usersQuery
    .Select(u => new Property { Value = new GuidsPropertyValue {
        GuidValues = u.UserRoles.Select(ur => ur.Role_ID)
    }}.Value);

(3)

usersQuery
    .Select(u => new Property { Value = new StringPropertyValue {
        StringValue = u.FirstName
    }}.Value);
